newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean firms to produce more high-end chips.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean firms to produce more high-end chips.

text.p: South Korean manufacturers are set to increase production of new, powerful computer chips to secure a foothold in the market for greater memory capacity.
Korea's second and third-ranked chipmakers, LG Semicon Co and Hyundai Electronics, said they would significantly expand their production of 64 megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips.
Analysts said the decision would improve long-term profit margins hit by plunging prices for 16-megabit DRAMs.
The 64-megabit chips will power a new generation of computers including super-computers, powerful workstations, notebook PCs and other information technology equipment.
"The domestic chipmakers are heading down the right track as they are not expected to make profits in 16-megabit sales," said Woo Young-moo of Daewoo Securities.
South Korea and Japan are the sole competitors in the 64-megabit DRAM market, while Taiwanese chip makers are now producing 16-megabit DRAMs.
LG Semicon Co said the company would raise its output of 64-megabit DRAMs to one million units a month by the third quarter of this year, from 150,000.
The LG Group affiliate earlier said it would reach that production level in the first half of the year.
"With the 16-megabit DRAM chips, we cannot expect good profit margins. But the 64-megabit DRAM will be more popular in the end of this year," said spokesman Han Dong-moon of LG.

Hyundai Electronics said it would raise its monthly output of 64-megabit DRAMs to 500,000 a month in the first half of this year and to three million a month by the end of the year. It currently produces 200,000 to 300,000 a month.
"We can be competitive when we have a monthly production capacity of three million," said spokesman Bang Min-ho of Hyundai Electronics, an unit of the Hyundai Group.
"We will control the output in accordance with world demand," Bang said.
LG and Hyundai Electronics said they sought to increase their global market share with Monday's move.

Top-ranked Samsung Electronics, the world's largest memory producer, said it had no immediate plans to raise its output of 64-megabit DRAMs, but analysts said Samsung would have little choice but to follow its competitors' lead.
Jon Chong-hwa of Hanuri Salomon Securities said: "As the nation's largest chipmaker, Samsung is unlikely to remain quiet in the face of the others' plans."

He forecast Samsung's monthly output of 64-megabit DRAMs would increase by three million in 1997 and seven million in 1998. He estimated production by LG and Hyundai this year at one million and two million, respectively.
"Samsung will follow suit. I have no doubt about it," said analyst Oh Jun-young of Dongbang Securities.
He said Samsung's current capacty is one million units.

Company officials said the unit price for 64-megabit DRAMs currently ranges between $50 and $54, compared to $10 for 16-megabit DRAMs. Semiconductors, including memory chips, are South Korea's single largest export item.
Company officials and analysts said the prices of 16-megabit DRAM chips have fallen to below $10 per unit on the spot market from about $50 last December.
Analysts forecast world demand for 64-megabit demand would not rise sharply this year.
"Production is not an issue but demand should be a major concern," Jon said. "Demand will rise only when the price of 64-megabit DRAM is below that of four 16-megabit DRAM."
At present, few computer manufacturers are using the 64-megabit DRAM chips in high-value-added computers including powerful workstations, analysts said.
